content.seoTitle: Flash Fiction Craft: What We Carried Out
content.seoDescription: Read an original flash-fiction story about evacuating a home under threat, plus a craft breakdown of urgency and pacing from a public writing prompt.

blocks.text: This piece answers a short writing prompt about an evacuation under threat, published in the DummyJSON placeholder-content API. The prompt is used only as a starting image; none of its wording or plot is reproduced below.

The county had given them twenty minutes, which Priya had learned meant twelve. She moved through the house the way she had practiced in her head a hundred times without ever believing she would need to: passports, the external drive, her son's inhaler, the box of letters her mother had never let her read while she was alive. She did not look at the orange light coming through the kitchen window. Looking at it would cost her a decision she didn't have time to make twice.

Her husband was outside coaxing the dog into the truck bed, the dog who had never once in six years gotten into that truck willingly, choosing, of course, tonight to remember every grievance it held against him. Priya counted the boxes at the door. Four. She had planned for five.

She found the fifth box in the hallway where she'd set it down to answer a call that didn't matter, and she carried it out past the dog, past her husband, past the mailbox that would or would not survive the night, and did not open it again until they were forty miles east and the radio had stopped saying their street's name. Inside was nothing she had packed. It was her son's crayon drawing of the house, taped shut in an envelope, put there by a nine-year-old who had planned better than either of his parents.

National Flash Fiction Day frames the form as a single scene compressed for emotional impact rather than a full account of events. Here, the entire evacuation stays inside one house and one twenty-minute window, so the reader experiences the same time pressure Priya does instead of being told about it afterward.

The Flash Fiction Institute's own definition of the form as a complete story in well under a thousand words means a countdown has to be felt through concrete objects — an inhaler, a box, a dog that won't cooperate — rather than through a stated clock. Those objects do the pacing work that a longer story might do with scene breaks.

Consistent with the Flash Fiction Institute's emphasis on omission, the story never says whether the house survives. That uncertainty is deliberate: the piece is about what a family chooses to save in twelve minutes, not about the fire's outcome, and resolving the fire would shift the story's attention away from the choice at its center.
Is this story based on a real evacuation?
No. It is original fiction written for this Signal Fiction series in response to a public API prompt about an evacuation scenario.
Why doesn't the story reveal what happens to the house?
Flash fiction's brevity works best when it resolves the character's internal choice rather than every external outcome, so the ending focuses on what was saved, not on the fire itself.
